title: State and metro employment: Second quarter 2026
gist: U.S. employment grew just 0.3% year over year in Q2 2026, and that thin national number masks a split labor market: 38 states added jobs while 12 states plus D.C. shed them, with D.C. down 4.8% and metro-level dispersion running from -3.2% (Waterloo-Cedar Falls, IA) to +5% (Sandusky, OH). The post is as much a FRED map-building tutorial as an analysis, and it explicitly warns that MSA figures carry large sampling error.

insights.claim: U.S. national employment grew only 0.3% year over year in Q2 2026, an acceleration from the prior reading but still a very low absolute rate of job creation.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A 0.3% YoY national jobs pace is near stall speed; it argues for a labor-market-driven easing bias and against cyclical exposure priced for a normal expansion.
insights.quote: National employment growth in the second quarter of 2026 accelerated slightly to 0.3% compared with one year ago.
insights.locator: National employment growth in the second quarter

insights.claim: Headline national employment growth conceals wide cross-state dispersion, so the aggregate print is a poor guide to regional labor conditions.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Regionally exposed businesses (banks, homebuilders, staffing, retail) should be underwritten on state-level employment, not the national number.
insights.quote: However, this aggregate figure conceals wide variation in job growth across U.S. states

insights.claim: In Q2 2026, 38 states added jobs year over year while 12 states plus the District of Columbia lost jobs — roughly a quarter of U.S. jurisdictions in outright employment contraction.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A quarter of the country already contracting on jobs is a recession-adjacent breadth reading even while the national aggregate stays positive.
insights.quote: 38 states experienced job growth, while 12 states plus the District of Columbia experienced job losses relative to one year ago

insights.claim: The median state grew employment about 0.4% year over year — above the 0.3% national rate — implying that large states are dragging the national aggregate down relative to the typical state.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Weakness is concentrated in high-employment-weight states, so national-aggregate-sensitive exposures are worse off than a state-count breadth screen suggests.
insights.quote: The median state experienced job growth of roughly 0.4%.
insights.locator: The median state experienced job growth

insights.claim: The District of Columbia posted the deepest state-level job loss at -4.8% year over year, an outlier roughly five times the next-worst jurisdiction, Montana at -1%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A -4.8% D.C. print points to a federal-government-linked employment shock; watch D.C.-area commercial real estate, government contractors, and regional banks.
insights.quote: The District of Columbia and Montana had the largest net job losses, at -4.8% and -1%, respectively.
insights.locator: The District of Columbia and Montana had

insights.claim: Nevada led all states with 2% year-over-year job growth and Minnesota followed at 1.4%, making the strongest state roughly seven times the national growth rate.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The best-performing states are still expanding at healthy rates, meaning the weak national number is a composition problem rather than a uniform slowdown.
insights.quote: Minnesota and Nevada had the strongest growth, with net job gains of 1.4% and 2%, respectively.
insights.locator: Minnesota and Nevada had the strongest growth

insights.claim: The post's claim that '25 states experienced growth above the median, highlighting growing resilience' is arithmetically empty — half of states are above the median by construction — so the stated resilience conclusion is not supported by that statistic.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Discount the optimistic framing and read the same data on breadth and magnitude instead; the tone of official data commentary can run ahead of what the numbers show.
insights.quote: Moreover, 25 states experienced growth above the median, highlighting growing resilience.

insights.claim: The median metropolitan statistical area added only 0.2% jobs year over year in Q2 2026, weaker than both the median state (0.4%) and the national aggregate (0.3%).
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Typical metros are closer to zero jobs growth than the state data implies — a signal for local-economy-levered assets like multifamily, small-cap regional lenders, and local services.
insights.quote: the median MSA experiencing a slight job gain of 0.2% in the second quarter of 2026 relative to one year ago
insights.locator: At the metro level, job growth on average

insights.claim: Metro dispersion spans more than eight percentage points, from Waterloo-Cedar Falls, Iowa at -3.2% to Sandusky, Ohio at +5%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Extreme MSA spread means location-specific underwriting dominates macro views for any locally concentrated asset.
insights.quote: The Waterloo-Cedar Falls, Iowa, MSA had the largest net job loss at -3.2%. In contrast, the Sandusky, Ohio, MSA had the strongest job growth, at 5%.
insights.locator: The Waterloo-Cedar Falls, Iowa, MSA had

insights.claim: The Fed authors explicitly caution that MSA employment figures swing sharply quarter to quarter and carry larger sampling errors than state and national data, and should not be over-interpreted.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Treat single-quarter metro extremes as noise; require multi-quarter confirmation before trading a local employment narrative.
insights.quote: These numbers tend to vary greatly from quarter to quarter, with even greater sampling errors than the errors at the state and national levels. So, be careful not to read too much into these data.
insights.locator: These numbers tend to vary greatly

insights.claim: The same state and metro employment maps can be rebuilt in FRED by searching total nonfarm employees for a state, choosing View Map then Edit Map, setting units to 'Percent Change from Year Ago' and quarterly frequency with 'End of Period' aggregation.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A free, repeatable way to refresh a state/metro labor breadth dashboard each quarter without a paid data vendor.

insights.claim: The authors bucket states into three color groups using thresholds of zero or below (job losses), below 0.4% (modest growth), and the remainder (strong growth) — effectively treating ~0.4% as the dividing line between weak and healthy state job growth.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit, Fed-authored benchmark for classifying a state's labor market; useful as a screening threshold for regional exposure decisions.
insights.quote: change the colors to red for states that shed jobs (or a value less than or equal to 0), light yellow for states with modest job growth (or less than 0.4), and dark green for states with strong growth
